definition: A way to invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals (usually monthly) instead of investing a lump sum. It builds discipline and uses rupee-cost averaging to smooth out market ups and downs.
Earning returns not just on your original investment, but also on the returns it has already generated. The longer money stays invested, the more dramatic the snowball effect becomes.

A stock's price divided by its earnings per share. It shows how much investors are paying for ₹1 of a company's profit — a rough, not perfect, gauge of whether a stock looks expensive or cheap versus peers.
The annual fee a mutual fund charges to manage your money, shown as a percentage of your investment. A 1% difference in expense ratio can cost lakhs over 20-30 years due to compounding.
The per-unit price of a mutual fund, calculated by dividing the fund's total assets (minus liabilities) by the number of units outstanding. It updates once a day, not continuously like a stock price.

How you split your money across asset classes like equity, debt, and gold. It is widely considered the single biggest driver of long-term portfolio returns — more important than picking the 'best' individual fund or stock.
3-6 months of essential expenses kept in a liquid, low-risk instrument (savings account, liquid fund) so a job loss or medical event doesn't force you to break long-term investments or take on debt.
Spreading investments across different assets, sectors, or geographies so that one bad outcome doesn't sink your entire portfolio. It reduces risk but does not guarantee against loss.

A mutual fund that simply holds the stocks in an index (like Nifty 50) in the same proportion, rather than trying to beat the market. Lower cost, no fund manager bias, and historically hard for most active funds to beat over long periods.
A 3-digit number (300-900) that summarizes your credit history. A score above 750 generally makes it easier to get loans approved at better interest rates.

A government-backed, long-term (15-year) savings scheme offering tax-free interest and a tax deduction under Section 80C. Very safe, but your money is locked in with limited partial withdrawal options.

A retirement savings scheme where both employee and employer contribute a percentage of basic salary each month. It earns government-declared interest and is one of the largest forced-savings tools for salaried Indians.
A voluntary, market-linked retirement scheme offering an additional tax deduction (up to ₹50,000 under Section 80CCD(1B)) beyond the regular 80C limit, with a mix of equity and debt exposure.

Pure life insurance that pays a lump sum to your family if you pass away during the policy term, with no maturity payout if you survive. It offers the highest cover for the lowest premium — the opposite of investment-linked insurance plans.

A plan that bundles life insurance with market-linked investment. It usually offers lower investment returns than a pure mutual fund and lower cover than pure term insurance because it's paying for both at once.

The rate at which prices rise over time, eroding the purchasing power of money. If your investments return less than inflation, you are technically losing real wealth even if the number in your account grows.
Your investment return after subtracting inflation. A fixed deposit earning 6% when inflation is 5% is only really growing your wealth by about 1% a year.
The total value of a company's shares (share price × number of shares). It's used to bucket companies into large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap — each with different risk and growth profiles.
Broad size buckets for listed companies. Large-caps are typically more stable and liquid; mid and small-caps can grow faster but swing harder in both directions, especially in downturns.

A mutual fund that invests in bonds and fixed-income instruments rather than stocks. Generally lower risk and lower return than equity funds, often used to park money for shorter time horizons or balance a portfolio.
A mutual fund investing predominantly in stocks. Higher potential long-term return than debt funds, but with higher short-term volatility — best suited for goals at least 5-7 years away.

Investing a large amount all at once rather than spreading it over time via SIP. Statistically it often outperforms SIP in rising markets, but SIP reduces the regret risk of investing everything right before a downturn.
The effect of investing a fixed amount regularly: you automatically buy more units when prices are low and fewer when prices are high, smoothing your average purchase cost over time.
A fee charged by a mutual fund if you redeem your units before a specified holding period (often 1 year for equity funds). It discourages short-term in-and-out trading of fund units.
A facility to automatically transfer a fixed amount at regular intervals from one mutual fund scheme to another — often used to move a lump sum gradually from a debt fund into an equity fund.
The reverse of a SIP: withdrawing a fixed amount at regular intervals from your mutual fund investment, commonly used to generate a steady 'income' in retirement while the rest stays invested.
The percentage of your total available credit card limit that you're currently using. Keeping it under ~30% is generally considered good for your credit score.
A debt mutual fund investing in very short-term instruments, used as an alternative to a savings account for parking money you might need within days to a few months.
Annual dividend per share divided by the share price, expressed as a percentage. It shows the cash return a stock pays out, separate from any gain or loss in its price.
A bull market is a sustained period of rising prices and optimism; a bear market is a sustained period of falling prices (commonly defined as a 20%+ drop from a recent high) and pessimism.
How much and how quickly an investment's price swings up and down. Higher volatility means bigger potential gains and bigger potential losses over short periods.
A statistical measure of how much a fund's returns have varied from its average return historically — a common, if imperfect, proxy for how 'risky' or unpredictable a fund has been.
A reference index (like Nifty 50 or Sensex) used to judge whether a fund or portfolio's performance is actually good, or just moving with the broader market.
The extra return a fund or investor generates above its benchmark index, after adjusting for risk. Positive alpha means genuine outperformance; most active funds struggle to consistently deliver it.
A measure of how much an investment moves relative to the overall market. A beta of 1.5 means the stock tends to move 1.5x as much as the market, in the same direction.
Tax on the profit made from selling an investment. In India, equity held over 1 year attracts Long-Term Capital Gains tax; held under 1 year attracts the higher Short-Term Capital Gains tax rate.

Profit from selling an asset held beyond the specified long-term holding period (1 year for listed equity/equity funds). It's taxed at a lower rate than short-term gains to encourage long-term investing.
Profit from selling an asset held for less than the long-term threshold (1 year for listed equity). Taxed at a higher rate than LTCG, which discourages frequent short-term trading.
An income tax section allowing deductions up to ₹1.5 lakh/year for investments like PPF, ELSS, EPF, life insurance premiums, and principal repayment on home loans.
A type of equity mutual fund that qualifies for Section 80C tax deduction, with the shortest lock-in (3 years) among all 80C options, making it popular for tax-saving plus growth.
A measure of risk-adjusted return — how much extra return an investment delivered per unit of risk taken. A higher Sharpe ratio generally means better returns for the volatility endured.
An open-ended fund lets you buy/sell units any business day at the current NAV. A close-ended fund has a fixed tenure and limited liquidity, typically trading on an exchange like a stock.

A direct mutual fund plan is bought straight from the AMC with no distributor commission, giving a slightly lower expense ratio and therefore slightly higher returns than the same fund's regular plan over time.
The company that manages and operates a mutual fund — e.g. it decides which stocks/bonds a scheme buys, within the fund's stated objective and regulatory limits.
The first-time subscription period when a mutual fund house launches a brand-new scheme. Unlike an IPO, buying an NFO doesn't make units 'cheap' — NAV simply starts at a base value like ₹10.
Periodically adjusting your portfolio back to your intended asset allocation (e.g. 70% equity/30% debt) as market moves cause the actual mix to drift away from your target.

Mapping specific investments to specific future needs (child's education in 15 years, house down payment in 5 years) rather than investing generically — it naturally guides how much risk to take for each goal.

How much volatility and potential loss you can tolerate, both financially and emotionally, without panicking and making poor decisions. It should shape your asset allocation more than recent market performance does.
A bank deposit for a fixed tenure at a fixed interest rate. Very low risk and predictable, but returns are fully taxable and often barely beat inflation after tax.
Paper-based ways to invest in gold without holding physical jewelry or coins — avoiding making charges and storage risk, while Sovereign Gold Bonds additionally pay a small fixed annual interest.
